title: The Biggest Show in Games
subtitle: Gamescom 2026 · Koelnmesse, Cologne
intro: Gamescom is the biggest games event on earth, and most people spend it standing in lines. This is the other way to do it: walk past every big queue, spend the day where you can actually play things and talk to the people who made them, and spend one queue at six o'clock when the crowd thins out.

dayGlance.title: In, and the scale of it
dayGlance.sub: 12:00 — the south entrance, then the big-publisher boulevard.

actsLede: Four acts, one building, no queueing until six.

acts.label: Act 1 · In, and the scale of it
acts.tagline: Walk the boulevard. Don't join anything.
acts.narrative:
Open outside the south entrance with the crowd behind you, then go in and walk halls 6 to 9 end to end without stopping for anything.

This first hour is reconnaissance, not content-gathering. You're doing two things: getting the scale on camera, and deciding which ONE big demo you care enough about to queue for tonight. Everything in these four halls runs a two-to-four hour line through the middle of the day. Walking past all of them is a deliberate decision, and it's the right one — say so on camera as you do it.

acts.label: Act 2 · Where you can actually play
acts.tagline: Hall 10, and the best conversations of the day.
acts.narrative:
Hall 10 is the one worth your afternoon. It's double-height and it holds the indie area, the retro machines and the careers section.

The reason it beats halls 6 to 9 is simple and it's your best line of the day: in the big halls you talk to hired staff in branded T-shirts, and here the person standing next to the screen usually made the game. Short queues, real answers, and people who are genuinely delighted anyone is asking. Then get outside for food at three, not one.

acts.label: Act 3 · Costumes and collectors
acts.tagline: Hall 5 — the best-looking hour of the day.
acts.narrative:
Hall 5 is where the show stops being about screens. The Cosplay Village is at the back of the lower floor, the merchandise is downstairs and Cards & Boards is upstairs.

This is your strongest visual material by a distance — months of work walking around asking to be looked at. One rule and it isn't negotiable: ask before you film anyone. Almost everybody says yes, and the ones who say no have a reason.

acts.label: Act 4 · The evening shift
acts.tagline: Six o'clock, when the queues finally break.
acts.narrative:
Day visitors start heading home around six and the lines in halls 6 to 9 drop noticeably over the last two hours. This is the window the whole day has been built around.

Pick the one demo you chose earlier and join it now. One, not three. And film the halls again on the way — the stands are built to be lit, so the same booth looks completely different at seven than it did at midday. Sign off inside, before they start clearing the building at eight.

kit: Camera plus TWO spare batteries — eight hours in there and sockets are basically nonexistent
Power bank for the phone; you'll be on the map and the app all day
A backpack is fine — no size limit. But every bag gets searched at the entrance, so a smaller one gets you in faster
Refillable water bottle — NOT glass. Glass bottles are banned on the fairground.
Earplugs if you own any — six hours of hall noise is genuinely punishing
preTrip: Screenshot your ticket — phone signal inside the halls is unreliable and you don't want to be reloading a QR code at the gate
Check whether your gamescom ticket covers VRS travel before you buy a train fare — it usually doubles as a free regional travel pass
Decide NOW which single big demo you'd queue an hour for tonight, and write it down
Pack the bag you actually need. Backpacks are allowed at any size; just expect it to be opened and looked through at security.
goldenRule: A big-publisher queue costs you three hours for fifteen minutes of playing. Skip them all. Play where the lines are short, talk to people who made things, and spend your one queue after 6 PM.

days.label: Gamescom
days.routeHeader: Brühl → Köln Messe/Deutz → south entrance → halls 6–9 → hall 10 → hall 5 → back to 6–9 → home

fullRoute.label: GETTING THERE
fullRoute.sub: Brühl to Köln Messe/Deutz — about 30 minutes, and likely free with your ticket

days.planHeader: Midday start, halls shut at 8 · Fri 28 August

planNote.text: Get to Köln Messe/Deutz — from Brühl that's roughly 30 minutes, usually via Köln Hbf and then one stop over the river. Check your gamescom ticket first: it normally doubles as a free VRS travel pass for the whole Cologne/Bonn region, so the journey may cost you nothing. The south entrance is about a three-minute signposted walk from the station. Public halls run 10 AM to 8 PM and today is a Friday, which is busy but not Saturday-busy. The single strategic call of the day: at midday the big-publisher demos in halls 6 to 9 are already running two to four hours, so do NOT queue this afternoon — walk them, pick one you actually care about, and come back for it after six when the crowd thins. Spend the middle of the day in hall 10, where the queues are short and the developers themselves are standing at the stands. Backpacks are fine and there's no size limit, but every bag is searched at the entrance so pack it to open easily — and no glass bottles. Eat at three, not at one — the food queues at lunchtime are worse than the game queues. One thing NOT to plan for tonight: the gamescom city festival is Saturday and Sunday only, at the Hohenzollernring and Rudolfplatz, so there's nothing in town this evening.

planArrival.title: Halls close at 8 PM
planArrival.note: Three minutes back to Köln Messe/Deutz and about half an hour home to Brühl, free again if your ticket covers it. Trains run late; there's no rush once you're out.

south-entrance.name: South entrance & getting in
south-entrance.angle: Cold open, outside, with the crowd
south-entrance.story: Film the opening out here before you go through security — the crowd streaming in is the shot, and you won't get it again. Then bag check and in. The south entrance is the one nearest the station and it's signposted the whole way.
facts: Gamescom is the biggest games event on the planet measured by how many people turn up — well over 300,000 across five days, from more than a hundred countries. Not the biggest in Europe. The biggest anywhere.

It's held in the Koelnmesse, one of the largest exhibition centres in the world, with more than a quarter of a million square metres of hall space. You will walk several kilometres today without ever going outside.

It's only been in Cologne since 2009. Before that Germany's big games show was in Leipzig, over in the east, and Cologne took it off them — which is still a slightly sore subject if you ask the right person.

routeCard.sub: Köln Messe/Deutz station · south entrance ≈3 min walk · 12:00
routeCard.note: Map pin is the station — the entrance is a short signposted walk from it. Backpacks are allowed at any size, but every bag is opened and checked, so pack it so it opens easily. Banned: glass bottles, anything sharp or pointed, and real or realistic-looking weapons (which matters for cosplay props).

planCard.todo: Cold open OUT HERE before security — the crowd is the shot. Two takes, then in. Have the bag ready to open.

boulevard.name: Halls 6–9 — the big-publisher boulevard
boulevard.story: Four halls of the companies whose games you've heard of, connected by one long boulevard. Walk the whole thing end to end without stopping. You're here to film the scale and to choose your one demo for tonight — not to stand in anything.
facts: These four halls are the big publishers, and the stands are not cheap. The larger ones cost more to build for five days than most people's houses cost to buy.

That queue you're looking at is real. A popular demo runs two to four hours through the middle of the day — for maybe fifteen minutes of actually playing. Deciding not to do that is the single best decision anyone makes at this show.

And notice what's being sold: almost nothing here is out yet. An entire hall of people being shown things they can't buy for another year. That's what a trade fair is — it was never meant for the public at all, and gamescom letting everyone in is the unusual part.

routeCard.note: Inside the halls — follow the overhead signage, not your phone. The map pin is just the Koelnmesse itself.

see: The main boulevard end to end
The queue lengths — film one honestly
planCard.todo: Reconnaissance only. Get the scale on camera, film ONE queue and say how long it is, and pick the single demo you'll come back for at six. Then walk on. Do not join anything.

indie-arena.name: Hall 10 — the Indie Area
indie-arena.angle: The person by the screen made the game
indie-arena.story: This is the best hour and a half of your day and the strongest material you'll get. Small studios, short queues, and developers standing at their own stands who will talk to you for as long as you want. Play three or four things. Ask people what their game is — they will light up.
facts: This is the Indie Area, and 'indie' just means games made by small teams instead of big companies. Sometimes that's ten people. Sometimes it's one person who has been at it for six years.

The Indie Arena Booth is one of the biggest shared stands at the whole show — dozens of tiny studios clubbing together to afford a space that none of them could pay for alone. That's the only way most of them get in the door here.

And this is why this hall beats the big ones: the person standing next to the screen usually made the game. You can just ask them about it. Over in halls six to nine you're talking to hired staff in branded T-shirts who got a briefing that morning.

routeCard.sub: Hall 10, upper level · indie area & Indie Arena Booth
routeCard.note: Hall 10 is double-height — indie and retro are up on the 10.2 level. Queues here are minutes, not hours.

see: Games you've never heard of, playable in minutes
planCard.todo: Actually PLAY things here — three or four. And talk to at least two developers on camera: ask what it is and why they made it. Best interview material of the day and it costs you no queueing.

retro-family.name: Hall 10 — Retro & Family
retro-family.angle: Machines older than most of the crowd
retro-family.story: Same hall, a few steps across: old consoles set up and switched on so you can play them. Visually it's the warmest thing in the building and there's almost never a wait.
facts: This is the retro and family section — consoles from the 1980s and 90s, plugged in and working, that anyone can walk up and play.
A lot of these machines still run because they were built to be opened and repaired. Plenty of hardware made in the last ten years won't be playable in thirty years' time, and these are.
It's also the quietest corner of the show with the shortest queues, which on a Friday afternoon in a building this loud is worth more than it sounds.

routeCard.sub: Hall 10, upper level · next to the indie area
routeCard.note: A few steps from the Indie Arena Booth — same level, same hall.

see: Kids playing games older than their parents
planCard.todo: Play one thing you recognise from your own childhood and say so on camera. That's the beat — nostalgia lands better than commentary.

outdoor-break.name: Outside — food and air
outdoor-break.angle: Eat at three, not at one
outdoor-break.story: Get out of the halls, eat, and let your ears recover. The outdoor spaces between the halls were expanded this year and there's a reopened area with a garden, a community wall and a beach-style bit.
facts: New for this year: they've opened up the outdoor space between the halls again — a garden area, a community wall and a section done out like a beach.
The practical reason you're eating now and not at one o'clock: food queues inside peak at lunchtime and they're worse than the queues for the games.
It's also the only place all day you can record clean audio. The halls are loud in a way that ruins anything you try to say to camera in them.

routeCard.sub: Outdoor areas between halls 6–9 · around 3:15 PM
routeCard.note: Food inside the halls is expensive and busy. Outdoor spaces sit between halls 6, 7 and 8 and alongside hall 9.

planCard.todo: Eat, drink, sit down. Record any piece-to-camera you've been saving OUT HERE where the audio is usable. Check the battery.

cosplay-village.name: Hall 5 — the Cosplay Village
cosplay-village.angle: Your best visuals of the day
cosplay-village.story: The back of the lower floor of hall 5. Months of work walking around in front of you, and people who built these costumes specifically to be seen. Take your time here — this is the footage that will carry the video.
facts: Cosplay is short for costume play — making and wearing the outfit of a character from a game, a film or a comic. Some of the things you're looking at took six months and cost more than the games they're from.
Gamescom hosts one of the biggest cosplay gatherings in Europe, and this hall is where people come to find each other rather than to look at stands.
The etiquette is simple and it matters: ask before you film or photograph anyone. Nearly everyone says yes — they made it to be looked at — but you ask first, every time.

routeCard.sub: Hall 5, lower floor, rear section · 4:00 PM
routeCard.note: ASK BEFORE FILMING ANYONE. It takes five seconds and it's the difference between being welcome here and not. Worth knowing on camera: props that look like real weapons aren't allowed through the entrance, which is why so much of what you'll see is oversized, brightly coloured or obviously foam.

planCard.todo: Ask first, every single time. Then ask them what it is and how long it took — that question gets you a real answer and a real face. Best sequence in the video.

cards-merch.name: Hall 5 — Cards, Boards & merch
cards-merch.angle: The bit of a games show with no screens
cards-merch.story: Upstairs in the same hall: board games and trading cards, with no electricity involved at all. Downstairs is the merchandise. Twenty minutes, walk-through pace.
facts: Upstairs here is Cards and Boards — board games and trading card games, in the middle of the world's biggest video game show, with not a screen in sight.
Trading cards have had an enormous few years, which is not what you'd expect at an event like this. Cardboard is doing fine.

The merchandise area downstairs is worth a walk even if you buy nothing. What people are willing to pay money for tells you which games actually have devoted fans, as opposed to just big marketing budgets.

routeCard.sub: Hall 5 · Cards & Boards upstairs, merchandise below
routeCard.note: Same hall as the Cosplay Village — no extra walking.

see: People playing board games at tables
planCard.todo: Quick walk-through. One line to camera on the oddness of cardboard thriving at a video game show. Don't linger — the evening window is the priority.

signings.name: Hall 11.2 — the signing area
signings.angle: The creators pull bigger queues than the games
signings.story: Where the people who make videos about games meet the people who watch them. You're not queueing — you're filming how big the queues are, because that's the actual story.
facts: This hall is the signing area, where video makers and streamers meet their audiences face to face.
Here's the thing worth saying out loud: for a big share of the people here, the creators are a bigger draw than the games. Some of these lines are longer than the ones for the demos.
Which is a genuine shift in how this industry works. Twenty years ago the game was the star. Now a lot of people come to meet the person who plays it.

routeCard.note: Don't queue. This is a filming stop, not a meeting stop.

planCard.todo: Film the scale of the queues and say the line about creators outdrawing the games. Thirty seconds. Then head back to halls 6–9 — your window is opening.

evening-halls.name: Back to halls 6–9 — the evening window
evening-halls.story: This is what you've been saving all day. Day visitors start heading home around six and the lines drop. Join the one demo you picked at lunchtime — and only that one.
facts: Most day visitors start leaving around six, and the queues in these halls drop noticeably over the last two hours. Same demo, a fraction of the wait.
So this is the moment to spend your one queue. One, not three — an hour in a line is fine when you've already got a day of footage; three hours is how people end up going home with nothing.
It also looks better now. These stands are built to be lit, and once the hall lighting takes over the same booth films completely differently than it did at one o'clock.

routeCard.note: The one demo you chose at lunchtime. Check the queue time before you commit — if it's still over an hour, walk and film instead.

see: The demo you actually came for
planCard.todo: Join ONE queue. While you wait, film the boulevard in evening light — it looks nothing like it did at midday. Get the demo itself on camera if they let you.

signoff.name: Sign-off, inside the halls
signoff.angle: Closing shot before they clear the building
signoff.story: Film your ending inside, with the hall still lit and still busy behind you. They start moving people out at eight and you do not want to be recording your closing line in an empty corridor.
facts: Halls shut at eight, so anything you still want on camera needs shooting before about twenty to.
Look back down the boulevard as you say it — eight hours ago you walked in at the other end of this building and hadn't seen any of it.
And the honest summary: the giant queues were never worth it. The day worked because it went where the queues weren't.

routeCard.sub: Anywhere on the main boulevard · by 7:40 PM
routeCard.note: Film it with the hall behind you while it's still full and lit.

planCard.todo: Closing shot, inside, hall behind you. Then stop filming and walk out before the crush.

home.name: Köln Messe/Deutz → Brühl
home.story: Three minutes back to the station, then home. Free again if your ticket covers VRS travel.

routeCard.sub: Köln Messe/Deutz · ≈3 min from the south entrance
routeCard.note: Roughly 30 minutes back to Brühl, usually via Köln Hbf. Everyone leaves at once at 8 — let the first crush go and you'll get a seat.

planCard.todo: Nothing left to film. Let the first wave go, then take the train home.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: The hook: 'this is the biggest games event on earth, and I'm going to get through the whole thing without standing in a single queue'
What this is: 300,000 people, eight halls, and a plan built entirely around not waiting in lines.
The promise: 'I'll spend the day where nobody else is looking — and queue exactly once, at six o'clock, when everyone else goes home'

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
signOff.where: On the boulevard, halls 6–9 — about 7:40 PM
facts: Where you are: the same boulevard you walked down eight hours ago, lit up and finally emptying out
The shape of the day: walked past every big queue, played a dozen small games nobody's heard of, met the people who made them, and spent the one queue at six when it was finally worth it.
The ask: like, subscribe — and tell me which game I should have queued for.

talkTipbox: Assume your viewer has never been to a trade fair and doesn't play games. Explain the words as you use them: indie means small teams, cosplay means costume play, a demo means a slice of a game that isn't out yet. The strongest thread you have is the queue decision — say at the start that you're not queueing and why, then pay it off at six. And in hall 5, ask before you film anyone. Every time.
goldenRules: Do not join a big-publisher queue before 6 PM. Three hours standing still is three hours of no footage.
Pick your ONE demo during the midday walk-through, and write it down.
Ask before filming anyone, especially cosplayers. Almost everyone says yes.
Your gamescom ticket usually doubles as a free VRS travel pass — check it before buying a train fare from Brühl.
Eat at 3, not at 1. Lunchtime food queues are worse than the game queues.
Backpacks are allowed, no size limit — but every bag is searched at the door, so pack it so it opens easily. No glass bottles.
Halls shut at 8. Be filming the sign-off by 7:40, inside, while it's still lit.
No city festival tonight — that's Saturday and Sunday at the Ring and Rudolfplatz.
Cosplay props: nothing real or realistic-looking as a weapon, nothing sharp or pointed. That rule is enforced at the entrance.
outro: The biggest games show on earth, done without standing in a single line until six o'clock.
